pages.h1: Websites and per-chair booking for barbershops in Wheaton, IL.
pages.lede: A shop with four chairs is four small businesses sharing a rent bill and a front door. The website, the booking and the client list have to work for the shop and for every barber standing in it.

sections.h2: Clients follow a person, and everyone in the building knows it.
paras: Somebody who's been sitting in the same chair for six years isn't a customer of the shop in any way that barber would recognize. He books around that barber's Thursdays, he waits when that barber is running behind, and if the chair moves eight blocks he moves eight blocks too. Pretending otherwise on your website is how you lose the argument later.

So the site says it out loud. Each barber gets a page with his own photograph, his own hours, the cuts he actually does and his own booking link — the client picks the man first and the shop second, because that's the order it already happens in.
bullets: A page per barber, with the work he really does
A booking link that only offers that barber's true availability
A shop-wide next available option for anyone with no preference
One phone number and one address, so the Google profile stays clean

sections.h2: When a barber leaves, the fight is about whose list it was.
paras: Booth renters own their relationships outright. Commission chairs are murkier, and most shops find out exactly how murky on a Tuesday when notice gets handed in. The part that stings is rarely the empty chair — it's that nobody left in the building knows which forty people used to sit in it, when they were last through the door, or how to reach any of them.

Appointments recorded in one ledger under the shop, with the barber as a field rather than as the owner, settles that quietly. The man who leaves keeps every relationship he built, which is fair and unavoidable anyway. The shop keeps its own history, which is the thing it's been paying rent on.

sections.h2: Four chairs means four sets of hours, and the calendar has to admit that.
paras: One man works Tuesday through Saturday. One does three long days and keeps Mondays for his kids. One takes appointments at seven in the morning before anybody else has a key in the door. A single set of shop hours posted on Google flattens all of it, and a client who turns up for a barber who isn't there blames the shop, not the barber.

Per-chair availability removes that phone call entirely. Somebody books on a Sunday night for a Wednesday at six thirty, the confirmation lands in about ten seconds, and the reminder goes out the day before without anyone touching it.

sections.h2: A first-timer picks a shop first and a barber second.
paras: He has no names yet. He has a phone, a lunch hour and three shops inside a mile, and he's looking at photographs of fades to work out whether anyone here cuts hair like his. Give him a straight price list, real pictures of your own work, and a booking button that doesn't demand he create an account first.
Then hand him to whoever's free. A first cut assigned well turns into somebody's regular, and a regular is a name in the ledger with a date attached to it.

paras: Foundation is $250 a month with a $250 setup: the website on your own domain, the Google Business Profile built out properly, booking synced to your Google Calendar, email at your own domain, and the search work so people looking for a haircut in Wheaton land on you. Growth is $500 a month with a $500 setup and adds review requests, the full client ledger, automated texts and emails, payments, expense tracking and monthly reports. Pay twelve months up front and it's $2,550 or $5,100, setup separate. Twelve-month partnership, billed the same date each month.

pages.townPara: Wheaton keeps two platforms on the Union Pacific West line — the downtown station at 402 Front St and College Avenue — which is unusual for a town of 53,970 and means the morning trade splits before it ever reaches your window. One chair fills with people who need to be gone by twenty past six. Another fills at ten with people who work from home now. A shop that publishes one set of hours and one number hides that difference. A shop that publishes each barber's real week lets a man book the person he actually sits with.

crmCallout.para: A CRM is nothing more exotic than the place your customer records live. Here it holds every cut, who did it, what it came to and when that client is due back — sorted by barber when you want it that way and by shop when you don't. When a chair turns over, whoever takes it inherits a list of names with dates on them instead of an empty week. The list is registered in your name, so it goes wherever the shop goes.

The barber keeps the relationships he built, which no software has ever changed. sections.h2: A commercial account is one contact and a garage full of vehicles.
paras: The person who calls you usually isn't the person who drives the van. She runs the office, she keeps a spreadsheet with plate numbers in it, and what she wants is for six vehicles to be looked after without her having to think about any of them. Every question she asks is really the same question underneath: can I stop tracking this myself.

So the account gets built the way she already thinks about it. One customer record, several vehicles under it, each with its own mileage, its own history and its own next due date, and one contact who gets told what's happening before it happens.
bullets: Vehicles grouped under a business, not scattered across driver names
Mileage and service intervals recorded per vehicle
One contact for approvals, whoever ends up dropping the keys
Invoices addressed to the company, with a reference number if they need one

sections.h2: Contractor trucks and church vans keep somebody else's calendar.
paras: A landscaping trailer can't be off the road in June. A van that carries a congregation on Sunday can sit in your bay all day Tuesday and nobody notices it's gone. Commercial scheduling is mostly knowing which of those you're holding, then booking the work into the week the customer can actually give up.

Online booking that offers real slots, with a reminder before the appointment, means she schedules at nine at night while she's doing the rest of her admin — instead of at ten in the morning while you're already under a hood with your hands full.

sections.h2: The invoice goes to a business, and the business has rules.
paras: Retail customers pay at the counter and drive off. Companies want an invoice with the vehicle on it, terms they recognize and a way to pay that doesn't involve coming back. Some want it monthly, all of them want it consistent, and any shop that has chased a commercial invoice knows the chasing cost more than the discount ever did.

Invoices go out the same day the vehicle leaves, payment happens online or at the counter into one ledger, and what's outstanding becomes a screen instead of a feeling. It feeds the monthly report and syncs to QuickBooks, so the year-end takes an afternoon rather than a weekend.

sections.h2: Service history has to outlive the driver.
paras: Drivers change. The van doesn't. Two years in, somebody new asks whether the timing belt has been done, and the honest answer is sitting in a paper folder that may or may not still be under the counter. A shop that can pull up every job against that plate in four seconds is a shop that keeps the account.

It's also where the next job comes from. A record showing the brake fluid was last changed at forty-one thousand miles is a phone call worth making at sixty-five thousand, and it's the rare call a customer thanks you for.

sections.h2: The call you missed was the one worth the most.
paras: A worried driver will call three shops. A fleet contact calls one, and if nobody picks up she moves down her list and doesn't come back — because what she's buying isn't a repair, it's not having to think about it.
For $100 a month every call gets answered, at nine at night or on a Sunday morning, with what was said and the number to ring back waiting for you before you lock up.

pages.lede: Almost nobody reads a paragraph about your salon. They look at a photograph, a star rating and how recent the last review is, and they've decided before they've read a word.

sections.h2: The map result is your storefront, and the site only confirms it.
paras: Search for nails near me anywhere in this town and what comes back is three listings with pictures on them. That panel does most of the choosing. The website's job is to survive the tap that follows — prices where a thumb can find them, a booking button that works one-handed, and photographs that match the ones on the profile.

Which is why the Google Business Profile isn't a box to tick after the site goes live. It's the first thing built and the thing that gets attention every week: categories, services, hours, holiday hours, and new photographs added steadily rather than in one burst the month you opened.

sections.h2: People choose a set from a picture, never from a description.
paras: Somebody scrolling for an ombre or a French tip is shopping with her eyes, and a stock photo of hands that aren't your hands gets clocked as a stock photo in about a second. Pictures of your own sets, taken in your own light, with the shape and color named underneath, do more for a salon than any sentence anyone could write for you.
It's also how you turn up in image results, and how a woman who found you on social media works out that the salon in the photos is the same one sitting on the map.

sections.h2: Recent reviews count for more than a big total.
paras: Forty reviews with nothing since last spring reads like a salon that might not be open. A steady trickle reads like a salon that's busy. The fix isn't asking harder, it's asking every single time, automatically, in the hour after the appointment while she's still looking at her hands.

On Growth that request goes out on its own, by text and by email, worded the way you'd word it. You never chase anybody again, and the number takes care of itself because it's asked of everyone rather than whoever you remembered.

sections.h2: The three-star review decides the people still deciding.
paras: Everyone reads the middle ones. A three-star note about a wait or a chip is where a careful person goes to learn what you're like when something goes wrong, and leaving it unanswered reads worse than the complaint did.

Answer plainly, own the part that's yours, say what you did about it, don't argue. If you'd rather that never sat waiting on your list, automated review replies are a $130 a month bolt-on and they go out in your voice, on every review, without you opening the app on a Sunday.

paras: Same salon name, same phone number, same address, same spelling, everywhere. Same service names in both places, so a search for a gel fill finds the thing you actually call a gel fill. Same hours, including the ones that change for a holiday.
It sounds like housekeeping, and it is. It's also the sort of housekeeping that quietly stops happening in month three, which is why it belongs to us rather than to you.

faqs.q: Can I show what things cost without publishing a full fee schedule?
faqs.a: Yes, and it's usually the better move. Publish what a first visit includes, how billing works for insured and cash patients and what happens if you don't take their plan. It answers the question people actually have without pinning you to a number that changes with the coverage.

faqs.q: Can patients fill in intake and insurance details before they arrive?
faqs.a: That's what digital intake is for. Forms go out with the booking confirmation, the patient completes them at home, and the carrier and member ID are sitting in the file before anybody has to verify anything. It usually saves the desk more time than the website does.

faqs.q: Does this replace the software we chart in?
faqs.a: No, and it shouldn't try. Clinical notes stay where they are. This handles the website, the booking, the reminders, the invoicing and the recall list — the administrative half that most practices are running out of a diary and somebody's memory.

pages.title: Landscape Design & Install Sites, Wheaton IL | Project Knox
pages.metaDescription: Websites, photo-led quoting, deposits and staged invoicing for landscape design crews in Wheaton, IL. Built for patios and plantings, not for mowing routes.
pages.h1: Websites and quoting for landscape design and install crews in Wheaton, IL.
pages.lede: A mowing account gets settled in one phone call. A patio, a planting plan and a drainage fix take three conversations, two visits and a deposit before anybody turns a shovel.

sections.h2: An install is a sale that happens over three weeks, not three minutes.
paras: Somebody has been thinking about the back of the house for two years. They'll look at your work, ask for a visit, get a number, go quiet for two weeks, talk it over at the kitchen table, and come back asking about a smaller version of the same idea. That isn't a lead going cold. That's how a big decision gets made in a household.

None of it survives a notebook on the dash. Every stage needs a record: the visit booked, the photographs taken, the number sent, the version they asked for instead, and the date you promised to check back.
bullets: A request form that asks for photographs and a rough measurement
A site visit booked into the calendar you already keep
The quote sent as a document rather than a text message
A follow-up reminder set the same day the quote goes out

sections.h2: A patio quote needs pictures before it needs a price.
paras: Nobody prices a slope, a drainage problem or a hundred feet of edging off a description given over the phone, and quoting blind is how a crew ends up eating a week in July. Asking for photographs at the enquiry stage does two jobs at once — it tells you whether the visit is worth the drive, and it tells the homeowner you're the sort of outfit that measures things.
Then comes the visit, the notes and a written quote with the work broken into lines they can move around. Line items are how a job survives a budget conversation instead of dying quietly in one.

sections.h2: Deposits and staged payments stop you financing the job yourself.
paras: Materials get bought up front. A crew gets paid every week. A three-week install with one invoice at the end means somebody else's patio is sitting on your credit line for a month, and everybody in this trade has done that at least once and sworn never again.

A deposit at signing, a payment when materials land, the balance at completion. Payment links go out with each stage into the same ledger as everything else, so what's outstanding is a number you can look at rather than a worry you carry around.

sections.h2: Your finished work is the proposal, so it has to be findable.
paras: Photographs of your own installs, sorted the way people search for them: patios, retaining walls, plantings, drainage. Before and after from the same corner of the yard. What the job involved and roughly how long the crew was there.

That gallery sells harder than any writing on the page, and it does it before you've spoken to anybody. It also settles the question every homeowner has and rarely asks out loud, which is whether you've built this exact thing before.

sections.h2: Nobody says no. They say not this year.
paras: Design work has a long tail. Budgets move, a bathroom gets done first, a job you quoted in April becomes real the following spring. A list of every quote sent, what it was for and when it went out is next season's work sitting in a file.

A short note in the autumn asking whether the patio is still on the list lands better than any advertising you could buy, mostly because they liked you the first time and nothing had gone wrong since.

sections.h2: The whole cost, in two lines.
paras: Foundation is $250 a month after a $250 setup and covers the website, the Google profile, booking, email on your own domain and the search work. Growth is $500 a month after a $500 setup and adds quoting and invoicing in one ledger, automated follow-up, online payments, expense tracking, monthly reports and a clean handoff to QuickBooks.
Bolt on 24/7 call answering at $100 a month if the phone rings while you're on a machine. Twelve-month partnership, same billing date every month, 15% off if the year is paid in advance.

sections.h2: Open the yard we built and send yourself a quote.
paras: Knox Blocks is a landscape business we built the whole way through. Request a quote as a homeowner would, then look at the record that request created. Four minutes will tell you whether this fits how you work.

pages.townPara: Cantigny Park sits at 1S151 Winfield Rd — the McCormick estate, the First Division Museum, formal gardens and golf — and people walk those beds all summer and drive home with something in mind. What follows a week later is a search, and it's never a search for mowing. Wheaton runs up against Glen Ellyn to the east, Winfield and Carol Stream to the north, Lisle and Naperville to the south, so a design crew's real radius crosses several town lines before the driving gets silly. The work has to be visible across all of them.

crmCallout.heading: Every property, every quote, every stage payment, on one screen.
crmCallout.para: A CRM is just the place your property, quote and customer records live. For install work that means the site visit, the photographs, the version they accepted, what's been paid and what's still due, filed under the address instead of scattered across three phones. Expenses go in the same place, so the patio that ran long is visible while you can still do something about it, and the monthly report tells you which kind of job is genuinely paying.

cta.heading: Request a quote from the demo and watch where it lands.
cta.para: It takes about a minute. If the shape of it looks like your work, we'll build yours the same way and you'll own every piece of it.

faqs.q: Can somebody request a design quote without me driving out there?
faqs.a: They can start one. The form asks for photographs, rough measurements and what they're picturing, which is usually enough to decide whether the drive is worth it and what to charge. The visit still happens, it just happens on jobs worth visiting.

faqs.q: Can I take a deposit and then bill the rest in stages?
faqs.a: Yes, on Growth. Deposit at signing, a payment against materials, the balance at completion, each one a link the customer can pay from a phone. All three sit under the same job, so you can see at a glance what a property still owes.

faqs.q: We do maintenance as well as installs. Does this handle both?
faqs.a: It does. Recurring accounts and one-off installs sit in the same ledger with different schedules, so the mowing route and a three-week build don't fight over the same calendar. Most crews run both, and the money side is where they get tangled.
